london_system.name: London System
london_system.summary: A solid, easy-to-learn opening. You play the same setup almost every game. Bishop out before e3 â€” that's the golden rule.
golden_rules: Bishop to f4 first, before e3. Always.
Don't trade your dark bishop unless you get something big.
Your dream setup: d4, e3, Bf4, Nf3, Bd3, O-O.
After setup is done, push for e4.

traps.name: Englund Gambit Trap
traps.description: They play 1...e5 trying to trick you. Take the pawn and win.
traps.trap_idea: They try to grab your b2 pawn with their queen. Let them â€” then trap the queen.
traps.how_to_avoid: Just play normal development. Their queen gets stuck.

traps.name: Bg4 Pin Trick
traps.description: They pin your knight spot with Bg4. You have a strong response.
traps.trap_idea: Push h3 then g4 to kick their bishop, then jump Ne5.
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't panic when they play Bg4. h3 then g4 is strong.

traps.name: Queen Trap after c5
traps.description: They take b2 with their queen. Nb5 and Rb1 traps it.
traps.trap_idea: Let them take b2. Their queen has no escape.
traps.how_to_avoid: Make sure you have Nb5 before allowing Qxb2.

d4.hint: What's the strongest first move to grab the center?
d4.right_feedback: Good â€” d4 grabs the center. Now think about your bishop.

d5.name: Main Line
d5.idea_opponent: They take their share of the center. Fair game.
d5.hint: Which piece should come out BEFORE you play e3?
d5.right_feedback: Exactly â€” Bf4 before e3. Golden rule of the London.
d5.wrong_feedback: In the London, the bishop MUST come to f4 before e3.

Nf6.name: Indian Setup
Nf6.hint: Same question as always â€” which piece first?
Nf6.right_feedback: Bf4 â€” doesn't matter what they play, bishop first.

c5.name: Early c5
c5.hint: They attacked your center. What's the calm response?
c5.right_feedback: e3 â€” stay calm. Your center holds.

Qb6.hint: Their queen eyes b2. How do you develop AND set a trap?
Qb6.right_feedback: Nc3 â€” if they take b2, Nb5+Rb1 traps their queen.

e5.name: Englund Gambit
e5.idea_opponent: A trick! They sacrifice a pawn hoping you blunder.
e5.hint: They offered a pawn. Should you take it?
e5.right_feedback: Take it. The Englund Gambit is bad for Black if you play correctly.
e5.wrong_feedback: Take the pawn! dxe5 is strong.

Bf5.name: Mirror London
Bf5.hint: They mirrored your London. Change your plan?
Bf5.right_feedback: e3 â€” stick to the plan. You have more space.

when_ahead.plan: Push e4 to open the center. Trade off defensive pieces.
ideas: Knight on e5 is a monster

when_equal.plan: Aim for e4. If blocked, play on the queenside with a4-a5.

when_behind.plan: Keep it closed. d4+e3 is hard to break. Wait for their mistake.

endgame_tips: d4+e3 structure is solid in endgames.
Activate your king early.
Push passed pawns.

london_system.black_plan: Challenge with c5 or Bd6, fight for the center, don't let White play e4 easily

italian_game.name: Italian Game
italian_game.summary: A classic opening. Develop quickly, point your bishop at f7, and attack the king. Simple and dangerous.
golden_rules: Bishop to c4 â€” aim at f7, the weakest square.
c3 prepares d4 â€” the ideal center.
Castle before attacking.
Don't grab pawns if it loses time.

traps.name: Fried Liver Attack
traps.description: Knight goes to g5 attacking f7. If they take, you sacrifice the knight for a devastating attack.
traps.trap_idea: After Nxf7, their king is dragged out. The attack is crushing.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should play d5 instead of allowing Ng5.

traps.name: Legal's Mate
traps.description: Sacrifice the queen to deliver checkmate with minor pieces.
traps.trap_idea: If they take your queen with Bxd1, you play Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5#. Checkmate!
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't take the queen if you see Bxf7+ coming.

traps.name: Blackburne Shilling Gambit
traps.description: Black plays Nd4 hoping you grab f7. Don't â€” just take the knight.
traps.trap_idea: Bxf7+ looks tempting but wastes your bishop. Nxd4 wins a piece.
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't be greedy. Nxd4 is simple and strong.

Nc6.name: Defending e5
Nc6.right_feedback: Bc4 â€” your bishop eyes f7.
Nc6.wrong_feedback: If you want the Italian Game, Bc4 is the move â€” aim at f7. Bb5 is the Ruy Lopez; d4 is the Scotch. Both fine, just different openings.

Bc5.name: Giuoco Piano
Bc5.hint: Prepare d4 with a pawn first.
Bc5.right_feedback: c3 â€” prepares d4. The big center is coming.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game, the idea is: c3 prepares d4 â€” that's how you build the big center. Playing d4 immediately lets Black trade with exd4, hitting your knight and equalizing. d3 (the Giuoco Pianissimo / Italian Modern) is the quieter alternative â€” also OK if you prefer slow play, but c3 is the classical main line.

Nf6.name: Italian Main Line
Nf6.hint: Now you can play the central break.
Nf6.right_feedback: d4 â€” supported by c3. Now the big center is yours.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game, d4 is the plan c3 was preparing. Anything else (b4 â€” Evans Gambit accepted is theoretically fine but a different opening; O-O â€” playable but lets Black play d6+ and consolidate) lets Black equalize.

exd4.name: Italian â€” d4 accepted
exd4.right_feedback: cxd4 â€” recapture with the c-pawn, building the big center.

Bb4+.name: Italian â€” Bb4+ check
Bb4+.idea_opponent: Black checks, hoping to disrupt your development.
Bb4+.right_feedback: Nc3 â€” block with the knight, accept the trade (or Bd2). Don't move the king.
Bb4+.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game after cxd4 Bb4+, Nc3 is the natural block â€” develops a piece AND meets the check. Bd2 (MÃ¶ller Attack variations) is also fine if you want sharper play. Don't play Kf1 (loses castling) or Kd2 (insane).

Nge7.name: Hungarian-like setup with Nge7
Nge7.idea_opponent: Unusual â€” knight to e7 instead of f6.
Nge7.right_feedback: d4 â€” punish the passive setup.
Nge7.wrong_feedback: Against Black's passive Nge7, d4 immediately is fine â€” Black can't easily challenge the center with the knight on e7 (blocks the e-pawn). Calm Italian setup play wins here.

Be7.name: Hungarian Defense
Be7.idea_opponent: Black plays the solid, passive Hungarian.
Be7.hint: Black's setup is too quiet â€” strike the center immediately.
Be7.right_feedback: d4 â€” open the center. The Hungarian doesn't fight for it; punish that.
Be7.wrong_feedback: Against the Hungarian Defense (...Be7), d4 immediately is the principled punishment â€” Black's quiet bishop on e7 lacks coordination with the rest of the army. d3 (slow Italian) is fine but lets Black equalize. d4 demands accuracy from Black.

Nf6.name: Two Knights Defense
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black plays more actively, eyes e4.
Nf6.hint: Black ignored f7 â€” punish it.
Nf6.right_feedback: Ng5 â€” attacks f7! Black must defend with d5 or face the Fried Liver.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Two Knights Defense, Ng5 attacks f7 directly. d3 is the quiet Modern Italian (safer); d4 leads to the Max Lange or Scotch Gambit transpositions. Pick your style â€” but avoid Nc3 which lets Black equalize easily with d5.

d5.name: Two Knights â€” d5
d5.idea_opponent: Black blocks the diagonal, counter-attacks the bishop.

Nxd5.name: Fried Liver setup
Nxd5.idea_opponent: Black recaptures with the knight â€” walks into the Fried Liver.
Nxd5.right_feedback: Nxf7! â€” the Fried Liver Attack. Black's king is exposed.
Nxd5.wrong_feedback: After exd5 Nxd5, Nxf7 is THE move â€” the Fried Liver. Any other move lets Black escape. The point: Black's knight on d5 IS undefended; Nxf7 forces Kxf7 (the king can't run), then Qf3+ regains material and continues the attack.

Na5.name: Polerio Defense
Na5.idea_opponent: Black hits the bishop, sidestepping the Fried Liver.
Na5.right_feedback: Bb5+ â€” check, keeps the bishop active.
Na5.wrong_feedback: In the Polerio, Bb5+ is principled â€” give check first, develop with tempo. Retreating with Bb3 or Bf1 loses tempo. d3 (Bd3 next) is the quiet alternative â€” playable but less ambitious.

Nd4.name: Fritz Variation
Nd4.idea_opponent: Black plays Nd4 â€” sharp, ambitious.
Nd4.right_feedback: c3 â€” kick the knight, regain control of the center.
Nd4.wrong_feedback: In the Two Knights Fritz Variation, c3 kicks the d4 knight. Nxf7 here is INCORRECT (the knight on d4 isn't undefended like in the main line). c3 first, then the position becomes tactical.

when_ahead.plan: Open the center with d4. Attack the king.

when_equal.plan: Control d4 and d5. Keep bishops active.

when_behind.plan: Keep pieces active. Look for tactical tricks.
ideas: Don't trade into a bad endgame

endgame_tips: Bishop pair is strong in open endgames.
Central pawns are powerful.
Activate rooks on open files.

italian_game_black.name: Italian Game (Black side)
italian_game_black.summary: How to defend against the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4) as Black. Two main systems: Two Knights Defense (3...Nf6 â€” sharp, attacking the e-pawn back) or Giuoco Piano (3...Bc5 â€” mirror the bishop, classical). Both are sound; choice depends on whether you want sharp or quiet play.
golden_rules: Against 3.Bc4, Nf6 (Two Knights) is the sharpest reply â€” counter-attack the e-pawn.
Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's bishop â€” solid, equal-ish.
Watch for the Fried Liver â€” d5 to block White's Ng5 is critical.
Don't play Na5 to chase the bishop unless you know the Polerio theory cold.

e4.right_feedback: e5 â€” accept the Open Game.

Bc4.name: Italian Game
Bc4.idea_opponent: White aims the bishop at f7.
Bc4.hint: Two Knights (sharp) or Bc5 (classical)? Nf6 is the most ambitious.
Bc4.right_feedback: Nf6 â€” the Two Knights Defense. Counter-attack e4. Sharper play ahead.
Bc4.wrong_feedback: Against the Italian (3.Bc4), Nf6 is the Two Knights Defense â€” counter-attacks White's e-pawn, leads to sharp tactical play (including the Fried Liver if White goes for it). Bc5 is the Giuoco Piano â€” mirror White's bishop, classical/equal. Both sound; Nf6 if you want sharper games.

Ng5.name: Italian â€” Fried Liver Attack
Ng5.idea_opponent: White attacks f7 with the knight!
Ng5.hint: Block the diagonal AND attack White's bishop. One move that does both?
Ng5.right_feedback: d5 â€” defend f7 by blocking the diagonal, AND counter-attack the bishop. The critical defense.
Ng5.wrong_feedback: Against 4.Ng5 (Fried Liver Attack), d5 is THE critical defense â€” blocks Bc4's diagonal at f7 AND attacks the bishop. Without d5, White plays 5.Nxf7 and your king is gutted. Other moves (Bc5, Nxe4) lose to the Fried Liver. d5 is mandatory.

exd5.name: Two Knights â€” d5 accepted
exd5.hint: DON'T recapture with the knight â€” that's the Fried Liver trap. Hit the bishop instead.
exd5.right_feedback: Na5 â€” the Polerio Defense. Attacks the bishop, sidesteps the Fried Liver.
exd5.wrong_feedback: After 5.exd5, Na5 (Polerio Defense) is the principled move â€” hits Bc4 with tempo, avoids the Fried Liver entirely. Nxd5 here is the Fried Liver trap â€” White plays Nxf7! winning material. Na5 is sound; Nxd5 is unsound unless you've memorized the Lolli/Traxler refutation lines.

d3.name: Italian â€” Modern (d3) / Giuoco Pianissimo
d3.idea_opponent: White plays the quiet Modern Italian â€” slow, positional.
d3.right_feedback: Bc5 â€” mirror White's bishop, classical setup. Equal positional game ahead.
d3.wrong_feedback: Against the Modern Italian (d3), Bc5 is the classical reply â€” mirror the bishop. d6 is also fine (Pirc-like). The Modern Italian is quiet; both sides have similar plans and the game is decided in the middlegame.

when_equal.plan: In the Italian as Black, the typical middlegame plan is queenside expansion (a6 + b5 + Bb7) while White attacks on the kingside. Trade pieces if needed.
ideas: Develop pieces actively, especially the c8 bishop via b7 or g4.
Castle kingside, then expand on the queenside with a6 + b5.
Watch for White's d4 break â€” meet it with exd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 cxd4 etc.

when_ahead.plan: Trade down. The Italian as Black usually reaches equal or slightly worse positions; if you're ahead, trade pieces and aim for the endgame.

when_behind.plan: Defend solidly â€” the Italian rarely produces forced losing lines from Black's side. Keep the position closed.

endgame_tips: Bishop endgames where you have the bishop pair are technically winning if you have any advantage.
Rook endgames after the Italian are often dry â€” know your Lucena and Philidor positions.

demands.character: Defensive, watchful â€” Fried Liver looms

sicilian_defense.name: Sicilian Defense
sicilian_defense.summary: The sharpest response to e4. You fight for the center with c5 instead of e5. Leads to rich, complex positions.
golden_rules: c5 fights for d4 without committing your e-pawn.
You're playing for a queenside counter-attack.
Don't be scared of White's kingside attack â€” you attack queenside.
d6 + Nf6 is the solid setup.

traps.name: Siberian Trap
traps.description: Black plays Qa5 pinning the knight and threatening Bxc3+.
traps.trap_idea: White's knight on c3 is pinned. If they don't see it, you win material.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should play Bd2 or Nb3 to break the pin.

traps.name: Magnus Smith Trap
traps.description: White plays Bc4 and after Bg7, Nd5! forks everything.
traps.trap_idea: The knight on d5 attacks multiple pieces. Black's in trouble.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should delay Bg7 and play a6 or e6 first.

e4.hint: What move fights for d4 from the flank, avoiding symmetry?
e4.right_feedback: c5 â€” the Sicilian. Most ambitious response to e4.
e4.wrong_feedback: In response to 1.e4, c5 is the Sicilian â€” most ambitious for Black, sets up unbalanced play. e5 invites the Open Game (Italian / Ruy Lopez / Scotch), e6 the French, c6 the Caro-Kann, d6 Pirc/Modern. All sound; c5 is the most fighting.

Nf3.name: Sicilian â€” Open setup begins
Nf3.idea_opponent: White's most popular move, preparing d4.
Nf3.hint: Flexible Najdorf-style setup â€” prepare Nf6 and later a6.
Nf3.right_feedback: d6 â€” supports e5 push, prepares Nf6.
Nf3.wrong_feedback: Against 2.Nf3, d6 is the most flexible â€” leads to Najdorf / Classical / Dragon depending on Black's later choices. Nc6 commits to the Classical / Sveshnikov lines. e6 leads to Taimanov / Kan / Paulsen. All sound; d6 is the most-played at top level.

d4.name: Open Sicilian
d4.right_feedback: cxd4 â€” trade pawns, open the c-file for queenside play.

Nxd4.name: Open Sicilian â€” Main
Nxd4.right_feedback: Nf6 â€” develop, attack the e-pawn.

Nc3.name: Open Sicilian â€” Nc3
Nc3.hint: Najdorf or Classical? a6 commits you to one of the most-studied openings in chess.
Nc3.right_feedback: a6 â€” the Najdorf. Prepare b5 + Bb7, fight on the queenside.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: In the Najdorf Sicilian, a6 prepares b5 + Bb7 â€” fighting on the queenside. Nc6 here would be the Classical Sicilian (different plan: knight to c6, dark-square strategy). g6 leads to the Dragon (sharp, double-edged). All sound; if you want the Najdorf, a6 is the move.

Be3.name: Najdorf â€” English Attack
Be3.idea_opponent: White plays the sharp English Attack â€” Be3, f3, g4, h4, attacking the kingside.
Be3.hint: Strike back in the center before White's pawn storm arrives.
Be3.right_feedback: e5 â€” closes the center, kicks the d4 knight, fights for d5 outpost.
Be3.wrong_feedback: In the Najdorf English Attack, e5 is the principled central break â€” closes the center BEFORE White's kingside storm gets going. Nf6 already played; e6 (Scheveningen-style) is playable but invites a faster White attack. e5 is sharp but theoretically sound.

Bg5.name: Najdorf â€” Bg5
Bg5.idea_opponent: White plays the aggressive Bg5 main line.
Bg5.right_feedback: e6 â€” solidify the kingside, prepare Be7.
Bg5.wrong_feedback: Against the Bg5 Najdorf, e6 is the most-played response â€” solid, prepares ...Be7. ...Nbd7 is also OK but less precise. e5 (which works against English Attack) is INFERIOR here because Bg5 pins the f6 knight and the e5 push isn't easily prepared.

c3.name: Alapin (2.c3)
c3.idea_opponent: White props the centre with c3, planning d4 â€” dodging the Open Sicilian.
c3.hint: Strike the centre at once, before White gets in d4.
c3.right_feedback: d5 â€” hit back immediately. With the pawn on c3, White can't develop the knight to c3, so your queen won't get chased after the trade.
c3.wrong_feedback: Against the Alapin, d5 is the most reliable â€” strike the centre while White's c3 pawn blocks the natural Nc3 development. Nf6 (inviting 3.e5) is the other main try, but d5 is the simplest equaliser.

exd5.name: Alapin â€” Main
exd5.right_feedback: Qxd5 â€” and here it's safe: White has no Nc3 (the pawn's on c3), so your queen sits comfortably. Develop next.

d4.name: Smith-Morra Gambit
d4.idea_opponent: White offers a pawn (2.d4 cxd4 3.c3) for fast development and open lines.
d4.hint: Take the pawn â€” but you don't have to keep grabbing.
d4.right_feedback: cxd4 â€” take it. If White then plays c3 (the Morra), you can decline the second pawn and just develop.

c3.name: Smith-Morra â€” declined
c3.idea_opponent: White offers a second pawn for a big lead in development.
c3.hint: Develop and hit e4 instead of getting greedy.
c3.right_feedback: Nf6 â€” decline cleanly. Develop and put a question to e4 rather than grabbing dxc3, which hands White exactly the fast, open game the gambit wants.
c3.wrong_feedback: Grabbing the second pawn with dxc3 is greedy and walks straight into the Smith-Morra: open c- and d-files, quick development, a real attack. Nf6 declines and keeps you solid.

Bc4.name: Bowdler Attack (2.Bc4)
Bc4.idea_opponent: White aims the bishop at f7 early, skipping the Open Sicilian.
Bc4.hint: Prepare to challenge that bishop with d5.
Bc4.right_feedback: e6 â€” prepares d5, which both hits the c4 bishop and grabs the centre. Simple and strong.
Bc4.wrong_feedback: Against the early Bc4, e6 is clean â€” it prepares d5, kicking the bishop and taking the centre. Don't rush ...e5 or leave f7 loose while the bishop stares at it.

ideas: Knights on c6 and d4 are strong

King activity is key.

caro_kann.name: Caro-Kann Defense
caro_kann.summary: A solid, reliable response to e4. You play c6 then d5, challenging the center while keeping a solid pawn structure.
golden_rules: c6 then d5 â€” challenge the center solidly.
Get your bishop OUT before playing e6 (same idea as London!).
Your pawn structure is your strength.
Don't rush â€” the Caro-Kann is about patience.

traps.name: Caro-Kann Smothered Mate
traps.description: White plays Nd6# â€” smothered mate! Black's pieces block all escape squares.
traps.trap_idea: The knight on d6 delivers checkmate because Black's own pieces block the king.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should not play Nd7 and Ngf6 without checking for Nd6.

e4.hint: What move builds a wall and prepares d5 with pawn support?
e4.right_feedback: c6 â€” the Caro-Kann. You'll play d5 with the c-pawn backing it up.

d4.name: Caro-Kann main
d4.right_feedback: d5 â€” challenge the center with pawn support from c6.

Nc3.name: Caro-Kann â€” Classical setup
Nc3.right_feedback: dxe4 â€” take the e-pawn, open lines for your light-square bishop.

Nxe4.name: Caro-Kann â€” Classical Main Line
Nxe4.hint: Now develop the light-square bishop â€” but where, before you lock in e6?
Nxe4.right_feedback: Bf5 â€” your bishop goes OUTSIDE the pawn chain, the defining Caro-Kann idea.
Nxe4.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Classical, Bf5 is the defining move â€” get your light-square bishop OUTSIDE the c6-d5-e6 pawn chain BEFORE you lock it in with e6. Playing Nd7 or Nf6 first traps the bishop inside the chain â€” the classic Caro-Kann mistake.

Ng3.name: Classical â€” Ng3 chasing the bishop
Ng3.right_feedback: Bg6 â€” keep the bishop's diagonal alive. Don't retreat further.
Ng3.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Classical after Ng3, Bg6 is correct â€” keeps the bishop active on the b1-h7 diagonal. Bd7 retreats too far (passive); Bh5? loses the bishop after h4-h5.

e5.name: Caro-Kann â€” Advance Variation
e5.idea_opponent: White locks the center, gains space, prepares kingside attack.
e5.hint: Get the light-square bishop OUT before you play e6.
e5.right_feedback: Bf5 â€” same defining idea as the Classical: bishop outside the chain before e6 locks it in.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Advance, Bf5 is the move â€” your light-square bishop MUST get out before e6 traps it. The Caro-Kann's main complaint about the French is the bishop-on-c8 problem; don't recreate it here. c5 (challenging the chain) is also fine but Bf5 first is more accurate.

Nf3.name: Advance â€” Short System
Nf3.idea_opponent: White develops calmly (the Short System), squeezing with space.
Nf3.hint: Your bishop's already outside the chain, so this is safe now.
Nf3.right_feedback: e6 â€” safe here because the light-square bishop is already on f5, not buried. Next build with Nd7, Ne7 and the c5 break.

Be2.name: Advance â€” Main
Be2.idea_opponent: White develops the bishop and castles.
Be2.right_feedback: c5 â€” hit the base of White's pawn chain (d4). This is Black's main freeing break in the Advance.

c3.name: Advance â€” c3 line
c3.idea_opponent: White supports d4 with c3 before developing.
c3.right_feedback: e6 â€” solidify with the bishop already out, then strike with c5 or bring the knight to e7.

exd5.name: Caro-Kann â€” Exchange Variation
exd5.idea_opponent: White trades and aims for a quiet game.
exd5.right_feedback: cxd5 â€” recapture with the c-pawn, leaving a symmetric structure.
exd5.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Exchange, cxd5 is correct â€” recapture with the pawn that has the better square afterward. Don't take with the queen (Qxd5 loses tempo to Nc3).

when_ahead.plan: Use your solid structure. Push pawns on the queenside.

when_equal.plan: Stay solid. The Caro-Kann is a fortress.
ideas: Knights on d5 or e4 outposts

when_behind.plan: Keep the position closed. Your structure is hard to break.

endgame_tips: Your pawn structure shines in endgames.
Bishop + pawns endgames favor you.
Passed c-pawn can be a winner.

french_defense.name: French Defense
french_defense.summary: Play e6 then d5. You let White take space but build a solid wall and counter-attack later.
golden_rules: e6 first, then d5 â€” challenge the center.
Your light bishop gets locked in. Find a way to activate it.
c5 is your key counter-strike against d4.
Be patient â€” the French is a slow burn.

traps.name: French Winawer Poisoned Pawn
traps.description: Black grabs the g2 pawn with Qg4. Risky but powerful if White doesn't know the theory.
traps.trap_idea: The g2 pawn is free and White's kingside is weak.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should protect g2 or play Qg4 prevention lines.

e4.hint: What move builds a solid wall, preparing d5?
e4.right_feedback: e6 â€” the French Defense. You'll strike with d5 next.

d4.name: French â€” Main
d4.right_feedback: d5 â€” challenge the e-pawn. White must commit to a setup.

Nc3.name: French â€” Classical / Winawer Setup
Nc3.idea_opponent: White defends e4 with a developing move.
Nc3.hint: Develop, attack e4. (Or Bb4 â€” Winawer.)
Nc3.right_feedback: Nf6 â€” Classical French. Pressures e4, develops naturally.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: After 3.Nc3, Nf6 is the Classical French (most-played, solid). Bb4 is the sharp Winawer (gives up bishop pair for activity and pawn structure damage). dxe4 is the Rubinstein (passive but sound). All defensible; Nf6 is the main line.

e5.name: French â€” Steinitz Variation
e5.right_feedback: Nfd7 â€” knight retreats but keeps c5 break available.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the French Steinitz, Nfd7 is correct â€” preserves c5 break. Ng8 wastes development; Nh5? loses to g4 trapping the knight.

Bg5.name: French â€” McCutcheon / Classical Bg5
Bg5.right_feedback: Bb4 â€” counter-pin, the McCutcheon Variation. Sharp but theoretically sound.
Bg5.wrong_feedback: Against 4.Bg5 in the Classical French, Bb4 is the modern main line (the McCutcheon). Pins the c3 knight. Be7 is the older, quieter Classical Main Line â€” also playable but less ambitious. Don't break the pin with h6 (it just helps White: 5.Bxf6 trades pieces).

Nd2.name: French â€” Tarrasch Variation
Nd2.idea_opponent: White avoids the pin, plays Nd2 instead.
Nd2.right_feedback: Nf6 â€” same development as Classical, but White's structure is different.
Nd2.wrong_feedback: Against 3.Nd2 (Tarrasch), Nf6 is the modern main line. c5 (challenging the center immediately) is also popular and sharp. Both are sound; Nf6 keeps options open.

e5.name: French â€” Advance Variation
e5.idea_opponent: White locks the center, plans kingside attack.
e5.hint: Challenge the pawn chain at its base.
e5.right_feedback: c5 â€” the standard French break, hits the base of White's pawn chain.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the French Advance, c5 is THE move â€” challenge White's pawn chain at its base (d4). Without c5 you're left passive with no counterplay. f6 is the alternative break (Milner-Barry-Gambit territory if White accepts), sharp and theoretically OK but less common.

exd5.name: French â€” Exchange Variation
exd5.idea_opponent: White trades and aims for a quiet game.
exd5.right_feedback: exd5 â€” symmetric structure. The Exchange is dry but not equal.

when_behind.plan: Keep it closed. Your pawn chain is hard to break.

Nf6.name: QGD â€” Main Line

Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the QGD, Bg5 is the main attacking move â€” pins the f6 knight, indirectly pressuring d5. cxd5 (Exchange QGD) trades immediately â€” playable, leads to a clear positional game. Bf4 is the London-style setup. For classical QGD, Bg5 is canonical.

h6.name: QGD â€” Tartakower / Lasker prep

h6.wrong_feedback: After Black's ...h6 in the QGD, Bxf6 is the main move â€” Black recaptures with the queen (Qxf6) or gives up the bishop pair entirely. Bh4 (keeping the pin) is also fine but committed.

dxc4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted (QGA)

dxc4.right_feedback: Nf3 â€” develop. The c4 pawn isn't going anywhere safely.
dxc4.wrong_feedback: In the QGA, Nf3 first is the modern way â€” develop before grabbing the pawn. Trying to win c4 immediately with Qa4+ is theoretically OK but creates an exposed queen. e3 (preparing Bxc4 next) is also fine. Develop, castle, THEN reclaim c4.

modern_benoni.black_plan: Fianchetto Bg7, play on the kingside with f5 or center with e5, use the dark squares

after_d6.key_decision: The Modern Benoni structure is set - asymmetric and sharp

e4.why_good: White has a strong center with d5+e4

czech_benoni.name: Czech Benoni
czech_benoni.white_plan: Build a big center (e4+d5), slowly expand, use space advantage
czech_benoni.black_plan: Lock the center with e5, maneuver pieces to the kingside, break with f5 when ready

after_e5.key_decision: The Czech Benoni - a closed, strategic battle

Nc3.why_good: Build behind the pawn chain, prepare f4

common_learnings: The Benoni creates an asymmetric pawn structure - White has space, Black has dynamics
In the Modern Benoni, the d5 pawn is both White's strength and a target
Black's dark-square bishop on g7 is crucial - don't trade it
f5 is the key break for Black in most Benoni structures
The Czech Benoni (e5) leads to a slower, more maneuvering game

budapest_gambit.name: Budapest Gambit
budapest_gambit.white_plan: Accept the gambit with dxe5, hold the extra pawn, develop solidly
budapest_gambit.black_plan: Sacrifice the e5 pawn for rapid development and piece activity, harass White's center

after_e5.key_decision: Black gambits the e5 pawn! White almost always takes.

dxe5.why_good: An extra pawn if White can hold it

budapest_main.name: Budapest Main Line (Ng4)
budapest_main.white_plan: Hold e5, develop with Bf4-Nf3-e3, maintain the extra pawn
budapest_main.black_plan: Pressure e5 with Ng4 and Nc6, develop Bb4+ for tempo, recover the pawn

after_Ng4.key_decision: Black immediately targets the e5 pawn

Bf4.why_good: The most reliable - holds the pawn and develops

e4.idea: Bold - give up e5 for a big center
e4.why_good: After Nxe5, White has a strong center

fajarowicz_gambit.name: Fajarowicz Gambit (Ne4)
fajarowicz_gambit.white_plan: Don't panic - develop normally with Nf3-e3, keep the extra pawn
fajarowicz_gambit.black_plan: Ne4 is more ambitious than Ng4 - aim for piece activity and tactical tricks

after_Ne4.key_decision: The Fajarowicz - trickier than the main line

Nf3.why_good: Don't overthink - develop and hold the pawn

Qd5.consequence: Black gets rapid development with tempo against the queen
Qd5.learning: Don't bring the queen out early to protect pawns - develop pieces instead

common_learnings: The Budapest is a surprise weapon - great for catching White off guard
Black sacrifices the e5 pawn for piece activity and development
Ng4 is the main move (more sound), Ne4 is the Fajarowicz (trickier)
White should stay calm, develop naturally, and hold the extra pawn
If White plays accurately, they keep a small edge - but practical chances are good for Black

demands.rewards_descriptor: tactical surprise and active piece play

dutch_defense.name: Dutch Defense
dutch_defense.white_plan: Control the center, develop naturally, exploit the weakened kingside (e1-h5 diagonal)
dutch_defense.black_plan: Control e4 with f5, choose between Stonewall (d5), Leningrad (g6), or Classical (e6+Be7)

after_f5.key_decision: Black plays aggressively with f5 - controlling e4 is the priority

g3.why_good: Bg2 will pressure the center and fight for e4

c4.why_good: Flexible - can transpose to many systems

stonewall_dutch.name: Stonewall Dutch
stonewall_dutch.white_plan: Fianchetto Bg2, exploit the weak e5 square, play around the stonewall
stonewall_dutch.black_plan: Build the wall: d5+f5+e6+c6, develop Bd6 and aim for a kingside attack

Nf3.why_good: The Ne5 outpost is White's dream square in the Stonewall

cxd5.why_bad: Opens the position for Black's bishops
cxd5.consequence: After exd5 or cxd5, Black's pieces become very active
cxd5.learning: Don't exchange in the center against the Stonewall - play around it

leningrad_dutch.name: Leningrad Dutch
leningrad_dutch.white_plan: Develop with g3-Bg2-Nf3, challenge the center, exploit the weakened light squares
leningrad_dutch.black_plan: Fianchetto BOTH bishops (Bg7 + f5), play for e5 break, kingside attack

after_Bg7.key_decision: The Leningrad setup - double fianchetto with f5

Nf3.why_good: Prepares to castle and fight for the center

common_learnings: The Dutch is aggressive for Black - f5 controls e4 and aims for kingside play
The Stonewall (d5+f5) creates a fortress but leaves e5 weak
The Leningrad (g6+Bg7+f5) is more dynamic with the double fianchetto
The weak e1-h5 diagonal is Black's main vulnerability after f5
Black should always castle kingside quickly to protect the weakened king position

four_knights.name: Four Knights Game
four_knights.white_plan: Develop all four knights, control the center, play d4
four_knights.black_plan: Mirror development, keep the center balanced

four_knights_game.name: Four Knights Game
four_knights_game.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6. Both sides bring both knights out â€” a calm, classical, very safe way to play 1.e4. Aim the bishop at b5 (Spanish-style), castle, and play a sound game with a tiny edge from the extra move.
golden_rules: Knights before bishops: Nf3 and Nc3 first, then decide where the bishop goes.
Bb5 copies the Ruy Lopez â€” it leans on the c6 knight that guards e5.
Castle early and keep the position solid; the Four Knights rarely blows up.
If Black pins your c3 knight with Bb4, you can mirror with Bb5 â€” symmetry is fine.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.hint: Develop the king's knight and hit the e5 pawn.
e5.right_feedback: Nf3 â€” develop and attack e5, the natural start.
e5.wrong_feedback: Start with Nf3 â€” develop a piece and put a question to the e5 pawn. That's the backbone of every 1.e4 e5 opening.

Nc6.hint: Bring the queen's knight out too â€” heading for the Four Knights.
Nc6.right_feedback: Nc3 â€” both knights out. This is the Four Knights, calm and solid.
Nc6.wrong_feedback: Nc3 develops your second knight and defends e4 â€” the Four Knights. (Bc4 is the Italian, also fine; Bb5 is the Ruy. For the Four Knights, Nc3.)

when_equal.plan: Finish developing and castle: Bb5 + O-O + d3 + Bg5. The Four Knights is a slow build â€” small, safe edges, no early fireworks.
ideas: Trade the b5 bishop for the c6 knight only when it wins something or wrecks Black's pawns.
Use the d4 or Nd5 break in the centre when your pieces are ready.
Keep the position symmetrical if you're happy with a small, safe edge.

when_ahead.plan: Open the centre with d4 once you're developed and use the extra tempo to push.
ideas: Jump a knight to d5 to pressure Black's position.

when_behind.plan: Symmetry is your friend â€” trade pieces and steer toward an equal endgame.
